name: Southwest Route

pitch_detail.notes: Loose scree and talus from Snowy Lakes basin up to the summit ridge
Short, exposed stem/mantle move across a gap to the true summit; often protected with a hip belay or short toprope; downclimbed or rappelled (~40 ft) on descent

rappel_detail.notes: The one rappel, about 40 ft (a 30 m rope is plenty), off the summit block across the exposed notch to regain the ridge. Then downclimb class 2-3 scree and talus toward Snowy Lakes.

rappels: One short rappel commonly used to descend the exposed notch just below the summit (rope carried mainly for this section); otherwise reverse the ascent gully.
descent_text: From the summit, most parties make a single short rappel (roughly 40 ft; a 30m rope is plenty) off the summit block to regain the ridge, then downclimb/scramble class 2–3 scree and talus back toward Snowy Lakes — plunge-stepping the loose scree speeds this considerably. From camp, retrace the PCT approach back over Granite and Cutthroat Passes to Rainy Pass.
approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Rainy Pass (4,880 ft) near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount. Park at the Rainy Pass North (PCT) trailhead. Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass (~6,800 ft), continue past Granite Pass (~6.25 miles in, where snowfields can linger into August) and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. About a mile before Methow Pass, a small, unsigned spur trail switchbacks up to Lower and then Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700–7,000 ft) — roughly 10–11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.
overview: A long, scenic PCT approach to a camp at Snowy Lakes, followed by an easy scree-and-talus scramble that ends in one short, exposed low-5th-class move to the true summit.
beta: The standard and by far most-climbed route on Golden Horn. From camp at Snowy Lakes, climbers ascend loose scree and talus on the mountain's southwest side to the summit ridge, then negotiate a short, exposed low-5th-class step — commonly described as a stem or mantle across a gap — to reach the small summit block. Many parties belay or protect the final move with a short rope despite its brevity, given the exposure below.
fa: Fred Beckey, Keith Rankin, and Charles Welsh, September 18, 1946 (first ascent of the peak)
